output.headline: Court holds luxury developer and facade contractor to account over Corniche window safety failings
output.bodyHtml:
A court has fined two companies a total of £1.3m over health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.

At a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Thursday, property developer St James Group Ltd was fined £1m and specialist facade contractor Lindner Prater was fined £300,000. Both firms were also ordered to pay costs of £125,000 each.

The firms were found guilty in August of ignoring “foreseeable risks” and convicted of “failing to discharge a duty” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when a window fell 26 storeys from the Corniche, a luxury development in Vauxhall, London, on 2 October 2018.

Ferris, who was a driver for Clarkes of London, had been returning to his coach when the window pane, which weighed 130kg and was roughly 85cm wide and 190cm tall, fell from around 90 metres (300ft).

The Corniche, on Albert Embankment alongside the Thames, features panoramic views over the Houses of Parliament. Luxury flats in the building – containing a gym, pool and spa – have been listed for sale at £3m.

Ferris’s widow, Rachel, said his death “could have happened to anybody” and “could have been prevented”.

In a statement read out in court, she said: “If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. One person could have asked: ‘Can’t we do this better?’ What those companies did killed my husband.

“Mick was just minding his own business. One minute there, one minute gone. The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child.”

The trial heard the design of the window in the Corniche was not safe because it opened outwards and was held in place by a single metal restrictor, so could be prised off by the wind.

Mr Justice Boyle said he was not sentencing the firms on the basis of the design itself being unsafe as they were “common within the industry” and there was no Health and Safety Executive (HSE) guidance prohibiting their use.

The judge said St James should have been more robust in “ensuring the critical safety component was present and engaged”.

The court heard during the trial that a window panel had previously fallen from the same development in August 2017, but that the design had not subsequently significantly changed.

Speaking outside court, HSE principal inspector James Goldfinch said Ferris “lost his life due to the failings of two leading companies in their field. The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near-miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling.

“For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary; for it to fall again was simply criminal.

A spokesperson for St James said: “The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge the court’s sentencing decision and the fine imposed.”
output.standfirst: Two firms convicted of health and safety breaches are sentenced in court. Mick Ferris was crushed to death when a 130kg pane fell 26 storeys from the Corniche housing development; the fines total £1.3m

output.headline: Andy Burnham begins to win progressives back to Labour, and tactical voting could put a majority within touching distance, poll finds
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, and progressive voters could put the party within touching distance of a majority and push Reform UK into fourth place if tactical voting is widespread at the next election, a major poll has found.

Those voters are motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.

The prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split, according to the poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, which also suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically.

It would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters. Such a tactic would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

Related: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

The poll on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour. It will encourage those in the party who are thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Since April, twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right.

Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees conducted the previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

If an election took place today, Labour would be the largest party in parliament on 272 seats, with a four-point lead, the research suggests. This would mean achieving 42 per cent of parliamentary seats with 28 per cent of the vote.

Reform would become the official opposition on 153. This represents 24 per cent of seats – the same as its vote share. The Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.

A two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats that are likely to decide a future election, because two hundred seats are tight marginals decided by under five points. But in a sign of the volatility of the polls, a far higher percentage of voters are open to tactical voting in those seats when they cite their preferred party.

Labour and the Conservatives would be favoured if voters are prepared to switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats, rather than their preferred party, with Reform UK’s seat count falling dramatically.

About 18 per cent of voters who live in a seat where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to do so but are not yet doing so. If those voters decided to vote tactically, Labour would have 319 seats – six short of a majority – and Reform UK would be reduced to 62.

Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour. The projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.

In 59 seats, Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points. Among these are the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – all of which have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives under a scenario with more tactical voting.

In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held Rawmarsh and Conisbrough with 49 per cent of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6 per cent. If tactical voting increases, the MRP gives Labour a 76 per cent chance of holding the seat; its base modelling indicates that Reform could win a tight race there, with a 51 per cent chance, but this plummets in the tactical voting scenario.

In Bassetlaw, tactical voting would lift Labour from 32 per cent to 40 per cent, so Reform could lose even as its own vote share rises from 35 per cent to 40 per cent. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place. The forecast estimates that the winner would shift from Reform, with a 77 per cent chance, to Labour, with a 58 per cent chance.

Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios, and under heavier tactical voting the chance of a Conservative win increases from 68 per cent to more than 99 per cent should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.

Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.

“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.

“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”

The sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year also complicates the prediction. Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to opt to vote for the Conservatives, even if they were technically the best placed to beat Reform at the next election, showing the limitations of predictions around tactical voting.

Labour is gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, but not from Reform, the poll also suggests. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60 per cent to 46 per cent; but on the right, of those lost to Reform or the Tories, it has fallen from 27 per cent to 24 per cent.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling indicated a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, but there was also significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.

“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”
output.standfirst:
Widespread tactical voting could push Reform into fourth place, polling suggests, though Labour would still fall short of a majority, with progressives motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage

• How Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

  • UK politics live – latest updates

output.headline: Police act on livestreamed footage to hold far-right activist Daniel Thomas over Channel dinghy
output.bodyHtml:
Police have acted on footage livestreamed by the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, arresting him on suspicion of “criminal damage with intent to endanger life”, after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was onboard.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said it had arrested a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”. Police said he remained in custody on Thursday.

The force had earlier said that it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he can reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety, but a French rescue worker had just got onboard.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on the larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. More than 200,000 people watched the livestreamed footage.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him that he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.

Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform. The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

The arrest came as the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings, responding to Home Office figures recording 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year.

The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small-boat arrivals in the UK.

A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020. But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”

Home Office data indicates that the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far, 18,565 including Wednesday’s arrivals, is down 42% on this time last year (32,188), and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).

Most small boats carrying asylum seekers across to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025. This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”
output.standfirst: The 37-year-old is in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life, after footage appeared to show him slashing a dinghy with a French rescue worker onboard

output.headline: Rory Stewart’s four-second gaze of absolute focus becomes a much-shared Newsnight meme
output.bodyHtml:
Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province. This week, he added a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: a beady, absolutely focused gaze at a fellow Newsnight panellist that lasted the longest four seconds in television history.

Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September, and in the last few days a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media.

Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI).

After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus.

Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme.”

Several friends texted him, which was how he first became aware of what had happened. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.”

He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.”

Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019.

“It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said.

Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added. He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera.

“This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.”

Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting.

The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place.

The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.”

Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”
output.standfirst: Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist Ailbhe Rea is shared widely online, as presenter Matt Chorley calls it ‘just quite a funny moment’

output.headline: UK data watchdog’s children’s data ruling against TikTok stands as it resumes algorithm inquiry
output.bodyHtml:
The UK’s data watchdog will receive a £12.7m fine from TikTok after the video app dropped its appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.

Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”

TikTok, which has more than 30 million users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.

Chinese-owned TikTok said it had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”, though it still disagreed with the ruling.

The Information Commissioner’s Office punished the video app in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform and failing to remove underage users.

When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.

The ICO said TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020. TikTok also failed to provide users with how their data was being collected and used, as well as neglecting to obtain parental consent.

At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.

“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.

Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.

The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has warned that “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. The country’s eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.
output.standfirst: TikTok drops its appeal and will pay the UK watchdog, which fined the video app £12.7m for failing to enforce its minimum age limit of 13 and remove underage users

output.headline: German prosecutors investigate man, 105, in judiciary’s drive to bring Nazi-era suspects to trial
output.bodyHtml:
German prosecutors have said they are investigating a 105-year-old man on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp.

The public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund is handling the case, which centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in western Germany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media.

The investigation is the result of an urgent, last-minute push by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war, on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role, were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims.

“The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said.

The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops.

The path to such cases was opened by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, which set a judicial precedent. He was convicted in 2011 of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there.

Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone.

Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison.

The Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial.

The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what the political theorist Hannah Arendt described as a Schreibtischtäter (desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that of Irmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder.

Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines after running away from her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial.

In June 2022 a court sentenced Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, to five years in prison for being an accomplice to murder. He died the following year, aged 102.

In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.

Dortmund prosecutors also opened a separate investigation last year into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944.

If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captive in Germany. More than half did not survive.
output.standfirst: Prosecutors in Dortmund, part of a judiciary racing to prosecute suspects before they die, accuse the centenarian of being accessory to multiple murders at Stalag 326 VI K in west Germany

output.trail: The current affairs show beats BBC’s Newsnight in the ratings, an early success that is a boost for ITV and improves the chance of its four-week run being extended

output.headline: UK inquiry puts TikTok’s handling of children’s data to the test of the law
output.trail: The UK inquiry is looking at whether the video-sharing app breaches data protection law in how it uses children’s data, putting TikTok under investigation

output.headline: Starmer presses Meta, TikTok, Google and X for real world changes at No 10
output.trail: In a Downing Street meeting with senior figures from the firms, the PM tells social media companies: ‘Things can’t go on like this’

output.headline: Data protection investigation could lead to £27m TikTok fine over children’s privacy
output.trail: Investigation finds the video-sharing app may have breached UK data protection law between 2018 and 2020 by failing to protect children’s privacy

output.headline: Molly Russell’s father sees inquest as ‘unique’ opportunity to make online platforms safer
output.trail: Ian Russell, speaking about the inquest into his daughter’s death, also says tech chiefs who endanger children should face prosecution

output.headline: Studies bring the effect of online beauty filters on children’s self-esteem into focus
output.trail: Studies suggest filters that ape the effects of cosmetic surgery are harming children’s self-esteem, as fears grow: ‘Teenage girls are feeling vulnerable’

output.headline: Information Commissioner’s Office puts TikTok and Reddit’s use of children’s data under scrutiny
output.trail: The UK watchdog says that by looking into the two sites plus Imgur it aims to learn about the wider market

output.headline: German court holds former Nazi camp guard, 101, to account for complicity in murders
output.trail: Josef Schütz is convicted and given a five-year jail sentence in Germany, though the former guard is unlikely to be put behind bars

output.headline: Guilty verdict holds Stutthof camp secretary accountable for complicity in 10,500 murders
output.trail: A court finds former Nazi camp secretary Irmgard Furchner, 97, who worked at Stutthof concentration camp during the second world war, guilty and hands down a two-year suspended sentence

output.headline: Trial begins for former Nazi camp secretary accused over murders of 11,000 people
output.trail: Irmgard Furchner, who tried to flee last month, goes on trial accused of complicity in killings at Stutthof death camp

output.headline: Friedrich Merz makes pope’s thinking on AI his holiday reading, passing over pacy potboiler
output.trail: The German chancellor packs the papal guide Magnifica humanitas, an AI encyclical, as his popularity stands at a record low

output.headline: Germany gives its spy agencies the reforms they asked for in security ‘revolution’
output.trail: Approved reforms lift curbs on the intelligence services and meet their wishlist; the agencies say Germany lags behind allies and enemies

output.headline: Minorities in Saxony-Anhalt speak out as they weigh their future before state election
output.trail: Polls point to the AfD, which promises deportations, winning Saxony-Anhalt – a first far-right state election win; minorities fear ‘this could just be the beginning’ and people face an agonising choice: stay or go
